chapter_title: Redis Replication: The Foundation of High Availability
chapter_summary:
Redis replication is the cornerstone of building highly available and scalable Redis deployments. At its core, replication allows you to create exact copies of your Redis dataset across multiple server instances. One instance acts as the **master**, handling all write operations and propagating changes to one or more **replicas**. Replicas, in turn, serve read requests, offloading the master and providing data redundancy. This master-replica architecture is fundamental not only for high availability but also for scaling read operations, as multiple replicas can serve concurrent read requests without impacting the master's performance. The beauty of Redis replication lies in its simplicity and efficiency.

When a replica connects to a master, it initiates a full synchronization process. The master creates a background RDB snapshot of its dataset and sends it to the replica. While this snapshot is being transferred, the master buffers all new write commands. Once the replica loads the RDB file, it then receives and executes all buffered commands from the master, catching up to the master's current state. After this initial synchronization, the master continuously streams all subsequent write commands to its connected replicas in real-time. This process is largely asynchronous; the master doesn't wait for replicas to acknowledge receipt or processing of commands before accepting new writes. This asynchronous nature ensures high performance on the master but introduces a slight potential for data loss in the event of a master failure before all commands have been propagated to replicas. However, for many use cases, the performance benefits outweigh this small risk, especially when combined with persistence mechanisms.

Configuring replication is straightforward. You designate one Redis instance as the master and others as replicas. To make a Redis instance a replica of another, you use the `REPLICAOF` command (or `SLAVEOF` in older versions). For example, if your master is at `192.168.1.100:6379` and you want to configure a new instance as its replica, you would run `REPLICAOF 192.168.1.100 6379` in the replica's `redis-cli` or add `replicaof 192.168.1.100 6379` to its `redis.conf` file. It's crucial to understand that a replica is read-only by default. Attempting to write to a replica will result in an error, which is a safety mechanism to prevent data divergence and ensure consistency with the master. While you can technically configure a replica to be writable (`replica-read-only no`), this is generally discouraged as it can lead to complex data consistency issues and is not recommended for most production scenarios.

Monitoring the health of your replication setup is vital. The `INFO replication` command provides a wealth of information about the master-replica connection, including the role of the instance (master or replica), the number of connected replicas, their IP addresses, ports, and the replication offset. The replication offset is particularly important as it indicates how far behind a replica might be from the master. A larger offset means the replica is further behind, which could be a sign of network latency or a struggling replica. For a master, this command shows the connected replicas and their status. For a replica, it shows its connection status to the master, the master's host and port, and its own replication status. Regularly checking this output helps identify potential issues like disconnected replicas or significant replication lag, allowing you to intervene before they impact service availability.

Common mistakes often include forgetting to set `replicaof` in the configuration file, which means the instance will start as a master. Another mistake is attempting to write to a replica, which will fail by design. Network connectivity issues between the master and replicas are also frequent culprits for replication problems, leading to replicas falling behind or disconnecting entirely. Ensuring proper firewall rules and network paths is paramount. Furthermore, it's important to understand that while replication provides redundancy, it doesn't automatically handle failover. If the master fails, a manual intervention is required to promote a replica to master, or an external system like Redis Sentinel is needed for automated failover, which we will explore in the next chapter. For safety, always ensure your master has persistence enabled (AOF or RDB) even with replication, as replicas only mirror the master's state, and without master persistence, a full system restart could lead to data loss if all instances are brought down simultaneously.

screens.title: Redis Replication — The Foundation of High Availability
screens.subtitle: How master and replica instances copy data, scale reads, and provide redundancy without blocking the primary

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn what Redis replication is, why it matters for availability and scaling, and how a simple master-replica architecture keeps data redundant and readable from multiple instances. Replication creates copies of a primary dataset on secondary instances so reads can be distributed and an outage of a single server is less damaging. You'll see the initial full synchronization that sends an RDB snapshot, how ongoing writes are streamed asynchronously, and how a replica’s read-only default protects data safety. We will walk through the commands used to configure replication, practical checks with the INFO replication output, and common mistakes like forgetting replicaof or attempting writes on a replica. A short hands-on lab demonstrates starting a master and two replicas, observing the sync, and validating that writes on the master show up on replicas while writes on replicas fail. By the end you'll understand the trade-offs of asynchronous replication: faster masters versus a small window of potential replication lag. Think about one question as we begin: how would you detect if a replica were falling behind in a production fleet?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Redis replication uses a master that streams writes to replicas after an initial RDB snapshot. Replicas serve reads and improve availability, but replication is asynchronous by default.

Redis Replication

Master-replica replication is the most direct path to read scaling and redundancy in Redis. This lesson combines concept, configuration, and a short lab to try on your machine.

Why it matters

Replicas let you serve more read traffic and provide copies of data for recovery, while keeping the master fast by streaming writes asynchronously.

In this lesson
Master-replica mechanics, REPLICAOF, INFO checks, and a local lab.
Coming up
Full sync, partial resync, and replication offset interpretation.
Master
Handles all writes and streams changes to replicas. Keep persistence enabled on the master for safety.
Replica
Serves reads and applies streamed write commands. Read-only by default to avoid divergence.
Initial Sync
RDB snapshot + buffered commands until the replica catches up.
Asynchronous
Writes are streamed without waiting for replica acknowledgement. Faster master, possible small lag.

Configuration
Use REPLICAOF or redis.conf to point replicas at a master and keep replicas read-only by default.
Synchronization
Initial RDB snapshot, buffered commands, then continuous streaming.
Monitoring

screens.title: What is Redis Replication?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and why it is the starting point for availability

narration.text: Redis replication is the process of creating copies of a Redis dataset on additional instances so that a single authoritative instance handles writes while others follow and apply the same commands. The master receives all write commands and propagates those writes to connected replicas. Replicas apply the commands and serve read requests, which reduces load on the master and increases the system's capacity to handle reads. The key behavior to note is asynchronous streaming: after the initial synchronization, the master streams write commands to replicas but does not wait for replica acknowledgements. This design favors master throughput and low write latency, but it also means there is a short window where recent writes may not yet be present on replicas. A concrete example: if a client performs SET user:123 "profile" on the master, that write is recorded on the master and streamed to replicas; a quick read from a replica may temporarily miss the value if the replica has not yet applied the streamed command. A common misconception is to assume replication provides automatic failover — it does not. Replication gives redundancy and read scaling, but promotion of a replica to master requires manual action or an external system such as Sentinel. Key takeaway: replication reduces master load and provides copies of data, but it is asynchronous by default and must be paired with monitoring and persistence to be operationally safe.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Replication copies a master's dataset to replicas by streaming write commands after an initial snapshot, enabling read scaling and redundancy.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is Redis Replication?
Definition

Master-replica copying

Replication copies a master's dataset to one or more replicas. After an initial sync, the master streams subsequent writes to replicas in real time.

Concrete example
SET user:123 "profile" on the master is applied and streamed. A read from a replica may briefly miss it if the replica hasn't applied the write yet.
Common misconception
Replication is not automatic failover. Replicas mirror data but promotion requires another tool or manual action.
Key takeaway
Replication improves read capacity and provides redundancy but is asynchronous by default, so monitor offsets and enable persistence on the master.
Quick visual
Master
Receives writes; streams commands to replicas.
Replica
Applies streamed writes, serves reads, read-only by default.
Why this matters

Replication is the simplest building block for high availability. It is efficient and lightweight, but requires monitoring and correct configuration to avoid surprises in production.

screens.title: Initial Full Synchronization
screens.subtitle: How a replica catches up when it first connects

narration.text: When a replica first connects to the master it performs a full synchronization, a multi-step handshake that ensures the replica starts with a complete, consistent dataset. First, the master creates a background RDB snapshot of its dataset. This snapshot is written to disk and then sent to the replica. While the snapshot is being produced and transferred, the master buffers any new write commands. Once the replica receives and loads the snapshot into memory, the master sends the buffered write commands so the replica can execute them and reach the master's current state. After this catch-up, the master switches to streaming every new write command to replicas in real time. A concrete example: starting a fresh replica for a dataset with many keys will trigger snapshot creation and can take time depending on dataset size and disk speed; the master buffers writes, which preserves ordering but increases memory and network load. A common operational gotcha is underestimating the snapshot cost on the master: a busy production master should be sized to handle snapshot creation and buffer growth, or use replication during off-peak windows. Key takeaway: the full sync ensures correctness, but plan for its resource and time cost when adding replicas.

keyIdea.title: Full Sync Steps
keyIdea.text: Master creates RDB snapshot, sends it to replica, buffers writes, then replays buffered commands so the replica catches up.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Initial Full Synchronization
Process Flow

Snapshot, Transfer, Buffer, Replay

1
Create RDB snapshot
Master writes a background RDB file of its current dataset to disk.
2
Send snapshot to replica
The master transfers the snapshot stream to the replica over the replication connection.
3
Buffer writes
While the snapshot is in transit, the master buffers new write commands to keep ordering.
4
Replay buffered commands
After loading the snapshot, the replica receives and applies buffered commands to reach parity.
Example
Adding a replica to a dataset with large keys will cause an RDB snapshot and transfer. Disk speed and network bandwidth directly affect sync time and buffer size.
Operational hint
Monitor master CPU, disk IO, and buffer growth during initial syncs. Consider scheduling replica additions during low traffic windows for large datasets.
Check after sync
Use INFO replication on both master and replica to confirm role, master link status, and replication offsets. A small offset difference is expected; large offsets indicate lag.

screens.title: Partial Resynchronization and the Replication Backlog
screens.subtitle: How Redis avoids full sync when a replica briefly disconnects

narration.text: Partial resynchronization helps avoid the cost of a full RDB transfer when a replica disconnects briefly and then reconnects. Redis keeps a replication backlog buffer on the master that stores recent write commands. If a replica disconnects and then reconnects quickly enough, it can request only the missing commands from the backlog, letting it catch up without downloading a full snapshot. This reduces network usage and lowers the master and replica load during transient interruptions. A concrete scenario: if a network hiccup drops a replica for a few seconds while only a small number of commands were issued, the replica can resume by applying those missing commands from the backlog and continue normal streaming. However, backlog size is finite; if the disconnection period is longer than the backlog covers, the replica must fall back to full synchronization. A common misconception is to assume partial resync always works — it only works when both master and replica still have the required backlog window. For operations, tune backlog size and monitor replication offset trends so you can detect when backlog misses are happening. Key takeaway: partial resynchronization optimizes short reconnections but is limited by backlog size and timing.

keyIdea.title: Partial Resync
keyIdea.text: A replication backlog stores recent commands so brief-disconnected replicas can request only missed commands instead of a full snapshot.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Partial Resynchronization
Mechanism

Backlog-based catch-up

The replication backlog stores recent write commands. If the replica reconnects within the backlog's window it requests only missing commands instead of repeating the expensive full sync.

Concrete scenario
A network hiccup drops a replica for a few seconds. The replica reconnects, uses the backlog to request the missing commands, and resumes without an RDB transfer.
Gotcha
If the disconnection lasts longer than the backlog window, the replica must perform a full synchronization and download an RDB snapshot.
Operational tip
Tune the backlog size to cover expected transient disconnects, and watch replication offsets to see when a replica falls outside the backlog window and triggers a full sync.
Checkpoints
  • Confirm replication uses backlog by checking logs or monitoring for fewer full-sync events.
  • Monitor replication offsets to detect backlog misses leading to full syncs.
  • Evaluate network reliability and adjust backlog size if short disconnects are common.

screens.title: Replica Behaviour: Read-Only by Default
screens.subtitle: Why replicas reject writes and the exceptions you should avoid

narration.text: By default Redis replicas are read-only to prevent data divergence from the master. Attempts to execute write commands on a replica will fail with an error. This behavior preserves a single authoritative source of truth and prevents conflicting writes that could make replicas differ from the master. You can change the default by setting replica-read-only no, but doing so is discouraged in production because it allows writes that will not propagate back to the master and can create hard-to-debug inconsistency. A concrete lab observation is instructive: after configuring a replica with replicaof pointing to the master, run SET anotherkey on the replica and you will see an error because the instance refuses the write. This is a deliberate safety mechanism. A common misconception is believing replicas accept writes and sync them back to the master; Redis replication flows from master to replica, not the other way around. If you need writable secondaries, consider other architectures or careful application-level reconciliation. Key takeaway: leave replicas read-only in production and rely on the master for writes to maintain a single consistent dataset. Replica Behaviour: Read-Only by Default means replicas block writes by default to prevent divergence; making them writable is possible but risky and generally discouraged.. In practical terms, why replicas reject writes and the exceptions you should avoid. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Replica Safety
keyIdea.text: Replicas block writes by default to prevent divergence; making them writable is possible but risky and generally discouraged.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Replica Behaviour
Comparison

Master vs Replica Writes

Default behavior
Replicas are read-only. Any attempt to write returns an error to protect consistency.
Making replicas writable
Setting replica-read-only no allows writes but can lead to divergent datasets and is not recommended for production.
Example
Try SET anotherkey on a replica and observe the error. This confirms the safety mechanism preventing local writes from diverging from the master.
Why this matters
Preserving a single write authority avoids conflicts and simplifies reasoning about data correctness across instances.
Operational rule
  • Keep replicas read-only in production.
  • If writable secondaries are required, plan for reconciliation and accept complexity.
  • Use replicas for read scaling, not write distribution.

screens.title: Configuring Replication with REPLICAOF
screens.subtitle: Commands and redis.conf snippets to create replicas

narration.text: Configuring a Redis replica is straightforward using the REPLICAOF command at runtime or the replicaof line in redis. conf for persistent configuration. To make an instance a replica of a master listening at 192.168.1.100 port 6379, run REPLICAOF 192.168.1.100 6379 in the replica's redis-cli or add replicaof 192.168.1.100 6379 to redis. conf before starting the server. The hands-on lab in this chapter uses loopback addresses for a local setup, but the same commands apply to remote masters. Remember that replicas are read-only by default; attempting to write on a replica yields an error. A common operational step is to verify replication status with INFO replication after issuing REPLICAOF to ensure master link status becomes connected and the replica begins synchronization. If you need to revert a replica back to a master, use REPLICAOF NO ONE. A misconception is thinking REPLICAOF immediately makes the replica identical; instead it triggers the initial synchronization flow which may take time for large datasets. Key takeaway: use REPLICAOF for quick runtime configuration and redis. conf for persistent setups, and always verify with INFO replication. Configuring Replication with REPLICAOF means use replicaof host port at runtime or replicaof in redis.conf; verify with info replication. use replicaof no one to stop replication.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use REPLICAOF host port at runtime or replicaof in redis.conf; verify with INFO replication. Use REPLICAOF NO ONE to stop replication.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Configuring Replication
Quick Commands

REPLICAOF and redis.conf

Use REPLICAOF at runtime for immediate configuration or add replicaof to redis.conf for persistent startup configuration. Always verify after configuring.

Example runtime command
REPLICAOF 192.168.1.100 6379
Example redis.conf line
replicaof 192.168.1.100 6379
port 6380
replica-read-only yes
Verification
Run INFO replication to check role, master link status, and connected replicas. Look for role:replica and master_link_status:up on a configured replica.
Operational note
To stop replication and make an instance a master, use REPLICAOF NO ONE. Keep replica-read-only yes to avoid accidental writes.

screens.title: Master-Replica Topology and Read Scaling
screens.subtitle: Architectural patterns for distributing reads and maintaining redundancy

narration.text: A common production pattern is one master with multiple replicas. The master remains the single writer and streams writes to each replica. Replicas serve read traffic, enabling horizontal read scaling: application instances route reads to replicas while sending writes to the master. This topology reduces master C P U and latency under read-heavy workloads and adds redundancy so that data persists across multiple nodes. However, because replication is asynchronous, replicas may lag behind the master by small amounts; therefore, strongly consistent read-after-write behavior typically requires reading from the master or using application-level techniques to verify freshness. Another practical consideration is network topology: place replicas in the same region as read-heavy services to reduce latency, but be mindful that cross-region replication increases lag and the chance of backlog misses. A common misconception is assuming many replicas eliminate the need for persistence — replicas are copies of the master's state and a master restart without persistence can still lose data. Key takeaway: use replicas to scale reads and add redundancy, but pair replication with persistence and monitoring for production safety. Master-Replica Topology and Read Scaling means one master, many replicas is the typical pattern for read scaling and redundancy, but plan for lag, persistence, and regional placement.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Topology Insight
keyIdea.text: One master, many replicas is the typical pattern for read scaling and redundancy, but plan for lag, persistence, and regional placement.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Master-Replica Topology
Architecture

Scale reads with replicas

Route writes to the master and distribute reads across replicas. This pattern reduces the master’s read load and improves throughput for read-heavy applications.

Placement tip
Put replicas near consumers for lower read latency, but expect more replication lag across regions.
Redundancy benefit
Replicas provide copies of data for fault tolerance, but they depend on master persistence to survive a full restart without data loss.
Example routing
Application writes go to master at 10.0.0.1:6379. Read requests are balanced across replicas at 10.0.0.2:6379 and 10.0.0.3:6379 to increase throughput and reduce master load.
Operational checklist
  1. Enable persistence on the master (AOF or RDB) so data survives a full restart.
  2. Monitor replication offsets and link status with INFO replication.
  3. Test read-after-write needs and route sensitive reads to the master when necessary.

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: Start a Master and Two Replicas
screens.subtitle: Configuration files, commands, and verification steps for a local setup

narration.text: This hands-on lab walks you through starting one master and two replicas on a local machine using three configuration files and redis-server. First, create a master config with port 6379, persistence filenames, and a data directory. Start it with redis-server redis-master. conf. Next create two replica configs with ports 6380 and 6381 and add replicaof 127.0.0.1 6379 to each. Start each replica with redis-server and confirm they begin syncing. After servers start, connect to the master using redis-cli -p 6379 and run INFO replication to see role:master and connected_slaves values. Connect to a replica with redis-cli -p 6380 and run INFO replication to see role:replica, master_host, master_port, and master_link_status. Test synchronization by setting a key on the master with SET mykey "Hello Redis!" and GET mykey on a replica to verify the value appears. Attempting SET on the replica will fail because replicas are read-only by default. These steps mirror the examples in the chapter and give you immediate, verifiable insight into how replication behaves in practice. screens.title: Using INFO replication to Monitor Health
screens.subtitle: What to read in INFO replication and how to interpret replication offset

narration.text: INFO replication is the primary CLI command to monitor replication state. When run on a master it reports role:master, connected replicas, and each replica’s IP, port, and state. On a replica it reports role:replica, the master's host and port, master_link_status, and the replica's replication offset. The replication offset is a numeric value representing how many bytes of write commands an instance has processed relative to the master. Comparing offsets between master and replica tells you how far behind a replica is: a larger offset gap indicates more lag and potential staleness. For example, if the master offset is 1500000 and a replica's offset is 1498000, the replica is behind by 2000 bytes of commands. This suggests network latency or processing delay. Regularly check INFO replication to detect disconnected replicas, large offsets, or master_link_status errors. A misconception is treating small offset differences as immediate failure — small lag is normal; the issue is persistent large offsets or increasing trends. Key takeaway: INFO replication and offsets give you concrete metrics to detect and respond to replication health issues before they impact users.

keyIdea.title: Monitoring Metric
keyIdea.text: INFO replication exposes the replication offset — use offset gaps to detect replication lag and investigate causes like network or resource constraints.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › INFO replication

Read replication state with INFO

INFO replication surfaces role, connected replicas, master link status, and offsets. Use it frequently to monitor health.

Example output (master)
# Replication
role:master
connected_slaves:2
slave0:ip=127.0.0.1,port=6380,state=online,offset=1498000
slave1:ip=127.0.0.1,port=6381,state=online,offset=1497990
master_repl_offset:1500000
Interpreting offsets
Offset gap equals master_repl_offset minus replica offset. A growing gap signals lag; stable small gaps are normal under load.
Actionable checks
  • Alert on master_repl_offset - replica_offset exceeding a threshold.
  • Investigate network, CPU, or disk IO if offsets grow consistently.
  • Check master_link_status on replicas; if down, replication is broken and requires reconnection or investigation.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Operational Checks
screens.subtitle: Frequent configuration errors and network issues to watch for

narration.text: Several mistakes frequently cause replication problems. First, forgetting to set replicaof in redis. conf or not issuing REPLICAOF leaves the new instance as a master, so you may unintentionally have multiple masters in your topology. Second, trying to write to replicas without disabling read-only mode leads to errors; conversely, making replicas writable can create data divergence. Third, network connectivity issues between master and replicas cause disconnections and can push replicas outside the replication backlog window, forcing costly full syncs. Common operational checks include verifying replicaof settings in configuration, ensuring firewalls and ports allow master-replica traffic, and monitoring INFO replication outputs for master_link_status and offset gaps. Another important check is enabling persistence on the master; without RDB or AOF you risk losing the authoritative dataset if all instances stop simultaneously. A misconception is that replication alone provides failover; it does not. For automated failover you must add a system like Sentinel or an external controller. Key takeaway: confirm replicaof is set, keep replicas read-only, monitor offsets, and ensure network paths and persistence are properly configured. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Common Pitfalls

Frequent causes of replication failure

Missing replicaof
An instance without replicaof starts as a master. Confirm configuration to avoid accidental masters.
Writing to a replica
Replicas are read-only by default. Attempts to write will fail. Making them writable risks inconsistency.
Network interruptions
Connectivity issues may cause replicas to fall behind or disconnect, possibly forcing expensive full syncs.
Checks to run
  • Confirm replicaof or REPLICAOF is set on replicas.
  • Verify open ports and firewall rules between master and replicas.
  • Use INFO replication to check master_link_status and offsets.
  • Ensure master persistence (AOF or RDB) is enabled.
Reminder
Replication provides redundancy and read scaling, but it is not equivalent to failover. Combine replication with Sentinel or other tools for automated promotion and complete availability plans.

screens.title: Testing Replication: Example Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A simple step-by-step verification from start to GET on a replica

narration.text: Walkthrough testing helps you confirm replication behavior and catch misconfiguration quickly. Start the master then each replica. After the replicas connect and finish their initial syncs, perform a simple write on the master and validate it appears on replicas. For example: after starting your master on port 6379 and replicas on 6380 and 6381, connect to the master and run SET mykey "Hello Redis!". Then connect to a replica and run GET mykey. If replication is working correctly, the replica returns the value. Next, attempt SET anotherkey on the replica; you should receive an error because replicas are read-only. Finally, run INFO replication on master and replicas and compare master_repl_offset with replica offsets. If offsets are close, replication lag is minimal. If there is a large gap, investigate network or resource issues. A common mistake is running these checks in the wrong order—verify master role and persistence first so you know you are testing against the authoritative source. Key takeaway: performing a small write-read test and checking offsets is an effective, low-risk way to validate replication in any environment. screens.title: Persistence and Replication: Why the Master Should Persist
screens.subtitle: Replication is not a substitute for AOF or RDB persistence

narration.text: Replication mirrors the master's in-memory dataset on replicas, but it is not a replacement for persistence mechanisms like RDB snapshots or AOF. If the master stops and has no persistence enabled, its dataset will be lost on restart, and replicas cannot recreate the lost in-memory state unless the replicas themselves also had a consistent persisted state. Because replicas simply mirror the master's current state, a master restart without persistence creates a situation where all instances may lose recent data. For operational safety, enable either RDB snapshots or AOF persistence on the master. The chapter advises ensuring master persistence even in replicated deployments. A practical example: if a power failure takes down the master and only in-memory state existed, even replicas cannot restore commands that were lost in memory—replication had no durable log of those writes. A misconception is assuming that because replicas exist, data will never be lost — replication helps availability but persistence provides durability across full outages. Key takeaway: always enable persistence on the master to avoid data loss in scenarios where all instances restart together. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Persistence & Replication

Durability versus redundancy

Replicas provide redundancy and read scaling, but persistence ensures data survives full outages and restarts.

Operational rule
Always enable RDB or AOF on the master even if you have replicas to ensure durability across full system outages.
Example risk
A master without persistence that crashes loses its in-memory dataset. Replicas cannot recover writes that were only in master's memory.
Checklist
  • Enable appropriate persistence mode on the master.
  • Test full restart scenarios to ensure data survives and replicas can resync.
  • Combine replication with monitoring and failover tools for full availability plans.
Takeaway
Replication improves availability and scale; persistence guarantees durability. Use both together for production-grade resilience.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the essential ideas to retain: master-replica architecture establishes a single writer and many readers; replication is asynchronous by default so the master streams writes without waiting for acknowledgements; full synchronization uses an RDB snapshot plus buffered commands to bring new replicas up to date; partial resynchronization leverages a replication backlog to avoid expensive full syncs for short disconnects. Replicas are read-only by default to prevent data divergence. Use REPLICAOF or replicaof in redis. conf to configure replication and verify state with INFO replication and the replication offset. Finally, ensure master persistence is enabled to preserve data durability even when replication is in place. Keep these concepts in mind as operational rules: configure carefully, monitor offsets and link status, and combine replication with persistence and failover tooling for complete availability strategies.

keyIdea.text: Replication provides read scaling and redundancy but requires monitoring and persistence for production resilience.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Key Concepts
Master-Replica
Master handles writes and streams them to replicas which serve reads and provide redundancy.
Asynchronous
The master does not wait for replicas, enabling high write throughput at the cost of potential small lag.
Full & Partial Sync
Initial full sync uses RDB + buffered commands; partial resync uses a backlog when possible to reduce overhead.
Summary takeaway

Use REPLICAOF to configure replicas, verify with INFO replication and offsets, keep replicas read-only, and enable master persistence for durable, reliable deployments.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three core reminders to apply in operations

narration.text: Keep three operational reminders front and center: configure replicas correctly with REPLICAOF and confirm with INFO replication; rely on replicas for read scaling but not as a substitute for persistence—always enable RDB or AOF on the master; and monitor replication offsets and link status so you can detect lag, backlog misses, or disconnections early. These three practices—correct configuration, durability, and monitoring—are the foundation of running replication safely in production. They prevent common mistakes like accidental extra masters, writable replicas that diverge, and surprise data loss after restarts. Ask yourself after any change: did I verify INFO replication, confirm persistence, and check offsets? If yes, you’ve applied the core operational discipline for Redis replication.
